newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Territorial dispute casts shadow over Bosnia peace.
newsitem.headline: Territorial dispute casts shadow over Bosnia peace.

text.p: Western powers are anxious to settle a volatile dispute over the Bosnian town of Brcko without upsetting the country's fragile peace process or relations within the NATO alliance, diplomats said on Sunday.
Fundamental disagreement between Serbs and Moslems over who should control the strategic northern town nearly caused peace talks to collapse in Dayton, Ohio in November 1995.
U.S. mediators decided to postpone the question altogether and leave it up to arbitration led by an American lawyer.
After months of delay, arbitration hearings were finally held this month in Rome under a strict media blackout.
The chief arbiter, Roberts Owen, must deliver a verdict by February 15, but diplomats say any decision will first have to prove acceptable to the major Western powers and Russia.

Diplomats say the United States, which dominated negotiations that led to the signing of the Dayton peace accords, was eager to avoid pushing through a solution to Brcko that would disturb trans-Atlantic relations.
Debates over how to halt the conflict in Bosnia led to discord between Washington and its European allies, and NATO countries want to keep avoid any repeat.
But as Western capitals weigh solutions for Brcko, the leak of an internal U.S. State Department policy paper has raised temperatures in the already heated atmosphere.
The policy paper, written by Assistant Secretary of State John Kornblum, favoured giving the town to Bosnia's Serb republic, provoking an uproar in the Moslem-Croat federation.
Bosnian Moslem officials, who see the United States as their main ally in the major powers' Contact Group, worried that Washington had adopted the European position on Brcko.

Federation officials warned such a solution would reward "ethnic cleansing", or expulsions of Brcko's mainly Moslem and Croat population during the war, but said they hoped Washington's proposal was merely a "trial balloon".
"There will be probably be more hints and rumours as we get closer to the deadline, as various solutions are tested to see how they fly," said one European diplomat.
With Bosnia-wide municipal elections planned for the spring, Western powers are eager to resolve the explosive issue of Brcko by the February deadline.
But the territorial dispute offers no easy solution and both sides are sticking to irreconcilable positions.

The Serbs, who seized Brcko early in the 1992-1995 war, insist the town must remain in the Serb republic because a corridor running through it is the only link between the Serb-controlled lands in eastern and western Bosnia.
They have threatened to go to war if the corridor is awarded to the Moslem-Croat federation.
Moslem leaders say the town belongs in the federation because Moslems and Croats formed a majority before 1992.
A senior Bosnian Serb official said he believed Brcko would be given to the Serb republic in the end but that there would be a degree of international administration.

"It appears the Americans have come around to thinking that any change in the status quo would cause instability, not just in that area but for the whole Dayton architecture," the official, who asked not to be named, told Reuters.
Bosnian Moslem political leaders have indicated their army is prepared to eventually fight to recapture Brcko. But the Serb official dismissed the possibility.
"Their threats of force mean less than our threats of force because Brcko is a matter of survival for us," he said.
Serb western Bosnia would be surrounded by potentially hostile federation territory and Croatia and cut off from Serbia to the east if Brcko passed into Moslem-Croat hands.

The nationalist Bosnian Serbs, who often fired on a weak U.N. peace force during the war, are relying on the long-term presence of combat-trained NATO troops enforcing the Dayton peace accords to protect them from a possible federation offensive against Brcko.
"The international community has invested so much in the peace process that it would not stand by and let it all be destroyed," said the Serb official.
